questions.t: An object's Default External Access can never be set more permissively than its Default Internal Access.
questions.f: An object's Default External Access can be set more permissively than its Default Internal Access, so partner users can see more than employees.
questions.x: Each object has separate internal and external organization-wide defaults, and the external value can never be more permissive than the internal one. Salesforce recommends setting every external default to Private.

questions.t: High-volume platform event messages are retained on the event bus for 72 hours.
questions.f: High-volume platform event messages are retained on the event bus for 24 hours.
questions.x: High-volume platform event messages stay on the event bus for 72 hours. The 24-hour window applies only to legacy standard-volume events defined before Spring '19, and new standard-volume events can no longer be defined.

questions.t: A before-save (fast field updates) record-triggered flow can change fields only on the record that triggered it.
questions.f: A before-save (fast field updates) record-triggered flow can update fields on related records as well as on the record that triggered it.
questions.x: Before-save flows support only Assignment, Decision, Get Records and Loop elements and can change fields only on the triggering record. Creating, updating or deleting related records requires an after-save path.

questions.t: Apex in an unlocked package version must reach 75% code coverage before the version can be promoted and installed in production.
questions.f: Apex in an unlocked package version must reach 85% code coverage before the version can be promoted and installed in production.
questions.x: Unlocked package versions need 75% Apex code coverage to be promoted and installed in production. Org-dependent unlocked packages skip the coverage check.

questions.t: Since June 26, 2026, Salesforce requires phishing-resistant MFA for privileged users such as System Administrators and users with Modify All Data.
questions.f: Since June 26, 2026, Salesforce requires phishing-resistant MFA for every user, including standard users with no administrative permissions.
questions.x: MFA is enforced for all users, but the phishing-resistant requirement applies only to privileged users: System Administrators and anyone with Modify All Data, View All Data, Customize Application or Author Apex. Other users can still use methods such as Salesforce Authenticator or TOTP apps.

questions.t: The Well-Architected Reliability pillar recommends treating 70% of a governor limit as the operational ceiling for a solution.
questions.f: The Well-Architected Reliability pillar recommends treating 90% of a governor limit as the operational ceiling for a solution.
questions.x: Reliability guidance tells architects to plan as if 70% of a limit is the practical maximum, leaving headroom for growth and spikes. Running up to 90% would leave far less margin than the framework advises.

questions.t: In the five-pillar Well-Architected Framework, the five-phase Agent Development Lifecycle sits under the Operational Excellence pillar.
questions.f: In the five-pillar Well-Architected Framework, the five-phase Agent Development Lifecycle sits under the Trust pillar.
questions.x: The Agent Development Lifecycle is part of Operational Excellence, alongside observability, DevOps and incident management. Trust covers agent permissions, auditing and security boundaries, not the agent build lifecycle.

questions.t: Salesforce suggests starting a new solution with the Trust and Reliability pillars as foundations before addressing the other three Well-Architected pillars.
questions.f: Salesforce suggests starting a new solution with the Operational Excellence and Fairness pillars as foundations before addressing the other three Well-Architected pillars.
questions.x: The framework treats Trust and Reliability as the base layer for new solutions, with the remaining pillars layered on after. Operational Excellence and Fairness are among the pillars addressed once that foundation is in place.

questions.t: In a record-triggered flow, invocable Apex actions can be called only from the after-save (Actions and Related Records) context.
questions.f: In a record-triggered flow, invocable Apex actions can be called only from the before-save (Fast Field Updates) context.
questions.x: Invocable Apex is limited to after-save record-triggered flows. Before-save flows are meant for cheap updates to the triggering record itself and cannot call invocable actions.

questions.t: In Flow Builder, Run and Debug always execute the most recently saved version of the flow, not unsaved edits.
questions.f: In Flow Builder, Run and Debug always execute the currently active version of the flow, not unsaved edits.
questions.x: Run and Debug use whatever version was saved last, even if a different version is the one activated for users. Activation only controls which version users run.

questions.t: The Salesforce Architects decision guide recommends Flow for record-triggered automation on objects with fewer than 15 automations per object.
questions.f: The Salesforce Architects decision guide recommends Flow for record-triggered automation on objects with fewer than 50 automations per object.
questions.x: The guide's density table treats fewer than 15 automations per object as low density, where Flow fits. Higher-density objects and complex cross-object logic are steered toward Apex triggers instead.

questions.t: In an Omni-Channel routing configuration, the queue with the lowest Routing Priority number is served first.
questions.f: In an Omni-Channel routing configuration, the queue with the highest Routing Priority number is served first.
questions.x: Routing Priority works in ascending order: a smaller number means the queue's work is distributed sooner. Omni-Channel also factors in how long items have waited and which queue members are available, but a higher number never jumps the line.

questions.t: When a custom Omni-Channel presence configuration is assigned to both a user and that user's profile, the user-level assignment takes precedence.
questions.f: When a custom Omni-Channel presence configuration is assigned to both a user and that user's profile, the profile-level assignment takes precedence.
questions.x: Presence configurations can be assigned to profiles or to individual users, and the individual assignment wins over the profile one. A user can only hold one presence configuration at a time, so adding them to another removes them from the first.

questions.t: With Omni-Channel skills-based routing, a record's required skills are evaluated when it enters a queue, so later edits to its skills have no effect until it is requeued.
questions.f: With Omni-Channel skills-based routing, a record's required skills are re-evaluated whenever it is edited, so later edits to its skills take effect immediately.
questions.x: Skills are checked at the moment a record lands in an Omni-Channel queue. Changing the skills afterward does nothing until the record is assigned to a queue again; if nobody qualifies, the item sits on the Skills Backlog tab.

questions.t: Agentforce Testing Center accepts up to 1,000 test cases in a single test.
questions.f: Agentforce Testing Center accepts up to 100 test cases in a single test.
questions.x: Testing Center caps a single test at 1,000 test cases, alongside a limit of 10 concurrent test jobs in a 10-hour window. A 100-case ceiling understates the limit tenfold.

questions.t: Agent tests should run in sandboxes with realistic data, never in production, because test runs can modify CRM records.
questions.f: Agent tests can run safely in production because test runs are read-only and never modify CRM records.
questions.x: The lifecycle keeps agent testing out of production since a test run can change real CRM records. Sandboxes with realistic data are the intended place for it, so the read-only claim is wrong.

questions.t: In the pro-code Agent Script workflow, activation, not publishing, is what makes a new agent version reachable by users.
questions.f: In the pro-code Agent Script workflow, publishing, not activation, is what makes a new agent version reachable by users.
questions.x: Publishing an Agent Script bundle only produces an inactive runnable version. Users reach it once it is activated as a separate step, so publishing alone does not put it live.

questions.t: A custom object can have at most 2 master-detail relationships, though it can have many lookup relationships.
questions.f: A custom object can have at most 3 master-detail relationships, though it can have many lookup relationships.
questions.x: Salesforce caps a custom object at two master-detail relationship fields, while lookups have no such small cap. Three is the number of custom detail levels allowed in a multilevel chain, not the per-object master-detail limit.

questions.t: Roll-up summary fields can be created only on the master side of a master-detail relationship.
questions.f: Roll-up summary fields can be created on the parent side of either a lookup or a master-detail relationship.
questions.x: Declarative COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX roll-ups are a feature of master-detail parents only. A lookup parent cannot host a roll-up summary field, which is one reason to pick master-detail.

questions.t: Converting a lookup to a master-detail relationship switches the child object's org-wide default to Controlled by Parent.
questions.f: Converting a lookup to a master-detail relationship keeps the child object's existing org-wide default, such as Private.
questions.x: Once the relationship becomes master-detail, the detail records take their access from the master, so the child's org-wide default changes to Controlled by Parent. Its earlier sharing setting does not survive the conversion.

questions.t: Batch Apex hands records to the execute method in chunks of 200 by default, and up to 2,000 when start returns a QueryLocator.
questions.f: Batch Apex hands records to the execute method in chunks of 2,000 by default, and up to 10,000 when start returns a QueryLocator.
questions.x: The default batch chunk is 200 records; a QueryLocator lets you raise it to at most 2,000. The false version inflates both numbers, and each chunk still runs as its own transaction with fresh limits.

questions.t: A synchronous transaction can enqueue up to 50 Queueable jobs, but an asynchronous transaction such as a batch can enqueue only one.
questions.f: A synchronous transaction can enqueue only one Queueable job, but an asynchronous transaction such as a batch can enqueue up to 50.
questions.x: The 50-job allowance applies to an ordinary synchronous transaction, while async contexts like batch are held to a single enqueued job. The false statement reverses which context gets which limit.

questions.t: Future method parameters are limited to primitives and collections of primitives, so records are passed as IDs and queried inside the method.
questions.f: Future method parameters can include sObjects and custom types, so records are passed directly instead of being queried inside the method.
questions.x: Future methods only take primitive values, arrays or collections of them; sObjects are blocked because the record may change before the method runs. Passing sObjects and custom types is a Queueable Apex capability, not a future method one.

questions.t: In the org-based development model the production org is the source of truth, while the package-based model makes the source control repository the source of truth.
questions.f: In the org-based development model the source control repository is the source of truth, while the package-based model makes the production org the source of truth.
questions.x: Org-based teams treat production as the authoritative record and ship changes together in one manifest-driven deployment. Package-based teams build scratch orgs from repository source, so version control holds the truth; the false statement swaps the two models.

questions.t: Lifecycle Center, formerly DevOps Center, is turned on from Setup in a hub org with no package to install.
questions.f: Lifecycle Center, formerly DevOps Center, is turned on by installing a managed package from AppExchange into a hub org.
questions.x: Lifecycle Center is built into the platform: you enable it in the hub org's Setup and nothing needs to be installed. The claim that it ships as an AppExchange managed package is wrong.

questions.t: Uninstalling an unlocked package deletes the components it contains, so package boundaries and deprecation plans need care up front.
questions.f: Uninstalling an unlocked package leaves its components in the org as unpackaged metadata, so package boundaries can be changed freely later.
questions.x: Removing an unlocked package removes its components along with it, which is why the article warns to plan boundaries and deprecation early. The components are not left behind as loose metadata.

questions.t: A synchronous Apex transaction can issue up to 100 SOQL queries, while an asynchronous transaction can issue up to 200.
questions.f: A synchronous Apex transaction can issue up to 150 SOQL queries, while an asynchronous transaction can issue up to 300.
questions.x: The per-transaction SOQL query cap is 100 in synchronous Apex and doubles to 200 in asynchronous Apex. The figure 150 belongs to the DML statement limit, not SOQL queries.

questions.t: A screen flow starts a new transaction each time the user clicks Next, so each screen's work gets its own set of governor limits.
questions.f: A screen flow runs as one transaction from its first screen to its last, so the work on every screen shares one set of governor limits.
questions.x: Each Next click in a screen flow begins a fresh transaction with fresh limits. It is an autolaunched flow, not a screen flow, that runs inside the launching transaction and shares its limits.

questions.t: Certified managed packages get their own allocation for most per-transaction limits, but CPU time is shared across the whole transaction.
questions.f: Certified managed packages get their own allocation for most per-transaction limits, but SOQL queries are shared across the whole transaction.
questions.x: Security-reviewed managed packages receive separate per-namespace counts for limits such as SOQL queries, up to a cumulative 11x cap. Heap, CPU time, execution time and namespace count remain shared by everything in the transaction.

questions.t: A Partial Copy sandbox can be refreshed every 5 days, while a Full sandbox can be refreshed every 29 days.
questions.f: A Partial Copy sandbox can be refreshed every 29 days, while a Full sandbox can be refreshed every 5 days.
questions.x: Partial Copy sandboxes hold a sampled subset of data and have the shorter 5-day refresh interval; Full sandboxes copy all data and wait 29 days between refreshes. The false statement swaps the two intervals.

questions.t: According to Salesforce Help, Full sandboxes are the only sandbox type that supports performance testing, load testing and staging.
questions.f: According to Salesforce Help, Partial Copy sandboxes are the only sandbox type that supports performance testing, load testing and staging.
questions.x: Salesforce Help reserves performance testing, load testing and staging for Full sandboxes, which copy all production data. Partial Copy sandboxes hold only a template-defined sample of data, so they are not the designated load-test environment.

questions.t: A newly created sandbox that is not activated within 30 days is deleted.
questions.f: A newly created sandbox that is not activated within 90 days is deleted.
questions.x: The activation window for a new sandbox is 30 days; after that, an unactivated sandbox is removed. 90 days is not the documented window.

questions.t: In Flow Orchestrator, an interactive step runs a screen flow and creates a work item, while a background step runs an autolaunched flow.
questions.f: In Flow Orchestrator, an interactive step runs an autolaunched flow and creates a work item, while a background step runs a screen flow.
questions.x: Interactive steps need a person, so they run an active screen flow and create a work item for the assignee. Background steps need no user and run an autolaunched flow; the false statement swaps the flow types.

questions.t: An orchestration fails if a step's flow receives more than 32,768 combined characters of input, so pass a record ID instead of a whole record.
questions.f: An orchestration fails if a step's flow receives more than 65,536 combined characters of input, so pass a record ID instead of a whole record.
questions.x: The documented input cap for a step's called flow is 32,768 combined characters, and passing whole records is the usual way to exceed it. 65,536 is not the limit.

questions.t: Orchestration steps that run at the same time are batched into one transaction, so their SOQL, DML and CPU time add up together.
questions.f: Orchestration steps that run at the same time each get their own transaction, so their SOQL, DML and CPU time are counted separately.
questions.x: Concurrent steps are grouped by user context and flow version and executed in a single transaction, so governor limit usage accumulates across the batch. Treating each step as its own transaction is the mistake the false statement makes.

questions.t: New cases need automation, such as an Apex trigger, to fill their Entitlement field; entitlements are not added to cases automatically.
questions.f: New cases get their Entitlement field filled automatically from the related account, so no extra automation is needed to apply entitlements.
questions.x: Salesforce does not attach entitlements to new cases on its own, which is why the Trailhead example uses an Apex trigger that looks up the contact and then the account. The false statement assumes an automatic default that does not exist.

questions.t: If no business hours are set, entitlement milestone timers use the org default of 24/7, so deadlines can expire overnight.
questions.f: If no business hours are set, entitlement milestone timers pause outside weekday working hours, so deadlines can expire only during the day.
questions.x: Without business hours, milestones fall back to the org default of 24/7 and keep counting through nights and weekends. They do not pause outside working hours unless business hours are configured.

questions.t: In the Lightning Service Console, records open as primary tabs and their related records open as subtabs.
questions.f: In the Lightning Service Console, related records open as primary tabs and the records they belong to open as subtabs.
questions.x: The console's tab model puts the main record in a primary tab and opens records related to it as subtabs underneath. The false statement inverts that hierarchy.

questions.t: Salesforce advises keeping an Agentforce agent to about 10-15 subagents, with no more than 15 actions per subagent.
questions.f: Salesforce advises keeping an Agentforce agent to about 10-15 subagents, with no more than 50 actions per subagent.
questions.x: The guidance caps actions at 15 per subagent because overlapping, cluttered options make classification less consistent. 50 actions per subagent is well beyond that recommendation.

questions.t: Rules that must always hold, such as refund eligibility, belong in Agentforce action code, filters or Agent Script rather than in agent instructions.
questions.f: Rules that must always hold, such as refund eligibility, belong in Agentforce agent instructions rather than in action code, filters or Agent Script.
questions.x: Instructions are natural language that the model interprets, so they are not deterministic and cannot enforce hard rules. Action code, filters and Agent Script run deterministically, which is why fixed rules go there.

questions.t: In the classic Agentforce builder, the reasoning engine picks a subagent using only subagent names and classification descriptions.
questions.f: In the classic Agentforce builder, the reasoning engine picks a subagent using subagent names, instructions and the full list of actions.
questions.x: Atlas classifies a request first, looking only at names and classification descriptions; instructions and actions are loaded after a subagent is chosen. That is why short, non-overlapping names matter.

questions.t: Salesforce treats it as ownership skew when a single user owns more than 10,000 records of one object.
questions.f: Salesforce treats it as ownership skew when a single user owns more than 100,000 records of one object.
questions.x: The ownership skew threshold Salesforce gives is 10,000 records of a single object owned by one user, the same figure used for parent-child skew. 100,000 overstates it tenfold.

questions.t: Lookup skew can occur on any lookup field, including custom ones, because it comes from record locking rather than the sharing model.
questions.f: Lookup skew can occur only under a private sharing model, because it comes from sharing recalculation rather than record locking.
questions.x: Saving a record locks the target of each lookup field, so many records pointing at one target contend for locks regardless of sharing settings. Unlike account skew, lookup skew is not tied to the sharing model.

questions.t: A user who must own very many records should have no role, or sit alone in a separate top-level role, to limit sharing recalculation.
questions.f: A user who must own very many records should sit at the bottom of the role hierarchy, under their manager's role, to limit sharing recalculation.
questions.x: Keeping a skewed owner out of the hierarchy, or isolated in its own top-level role, avoids recalculating access for everyone above them. Placing them beneath a manager adds more users whose access must be updated when ownership or roles change.

questions.t: An object starts with 25 roll-up summary fields; Salesforce Support can raise that, but 40 per object is the hard maximum.
questions.f: An object starts with 25 roll-up summary fields; Salesforce Support can raise that, but 100 per object is the hard maximum.
questions.x: The default allocation is 25 per object and Support can increase it only up to a hard ceiling of 40. A 100-field ceiling does not exist.

questions.t: Roll-up summary fields offer COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX, with no native average.
questions.f: Roll-up summary fields offer COUNT, SUM, AVERAGE and MAX, with no native minimum.
questions.x: The four roll-up types are COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX. Averages are not available natively, while MIN is, so the false statement swaps the supported and missing operations.

questions.t: After a detail record saves, its parent's roll-up is recalculated and the parent saves, which can cascade to a grandparent's roll-up.
questions.f: After a detail record saves, its parent's roll-up is recalculated by a nightly batch job, so a grandparent's roll-up updates the next day.
questions.x: Roll-up recalculation is a step in the save order of execution: the parent is recalculated and saved right away, and a change there can trigger the grandparent's roll-up in turn. There is no nightly batch for native roll-ups.

questions.t: Since API version 24.0, Apex test methods see only the data they create, apart from setup objects such as User and Profile, unless SeeAllData=true is set.
questions.f: Since API version 24.0, Apex test methods see all existing org records by default, unless the class is annotated with SeeAllData=false.
questions.x: Tests are isolated from org data by default; only a few setup-style objects stay visible, and SeeAllData=true is the opt-in to see the rest. The false statement reverses the default.

questions.t: Asynchronous jobs enqueued after Test.startTest() are executed synchronously when Test.stopTest() is called, so a test can assert on their results.
questions.f: Asynchronous jobs enqueued after Test.startTest() run in the background after the test method ends, so a test can only check that they were queued.
questions.x: Test.stopTest() collects the future, Queueable and batch work enqueued since startTest and runs it synchronously, which is how tests verify async Apex. They do not run later in the background.

questions.t: Changes a test method makes to records created in @TestSetup are rolled back when that method ends, so each method sees the original data.
questions.f: Changes a test method makes to records created in @TestSetup carry over to later test methods, so each method sees the previous method's edits.
questions.x: Each test method runs in its own transaction and its changes to the shared setup records are rolled back afterwards. Later methods therefore start from the data exactly as @TestSetup created it.

questions.t: When DML affects more than 200 records, an Apex trigger runs once per batch of 200, and Trigger.size reports only the current batch.
questions.f: When DML affects more than 2,000 records, an Apex trigger runs once per batch of 2,000, and Trigger.size reports only the current batch.
questions.x: Trigger invocations are chunked at 200 records, so a large DML operation fires the trigger several times and Trigger.size counts only the batch at hand. 2,000 is not the trigger batch size.

questions.t: Field changes made to Trigger.new in a before trigger are saved without a separate DML statement.
questions.f: Field changes made to Trigger.new in an after trigger are saved without a separate DML statement.
questions.x: Before triggers run before the save, so values set on Trigger.new persist automatically. In after triggers the triggering records are read-only, so that is the wrong context for such edits.

questions.t: If a bulk API call fires a trigger, valid records can save while failing ones are rejected; if Apex DML fires it, one error rolls back the whole operation.
questions.f: If Apex DML fires a trigger, valid records can save while failing ones are rejected; if a bulk API call fires it, one error rolls back the whole operation.
questions.x: Partial success is the behaviour for bulk API calls, whereas Apex DML is all-or-nothing when a trigger throws an error. The false statement swaps the two callers.

questions.t: Change sets can move only between orgs affiliated with the same production org, such as production and one of its sandboxes.
questions.f: Change sets can move between any two Salesforce orgs, such as two separate production orgs, once a deployment connection is set up.
questions.x: Deployment connections can link only orgs that share a production org, like production and its sandboxes or two sibling sandboxes. Unrelated orgs, including separate production orgs, cannot exchange change sets.

questions.t: An inbound or outbound change set can hold up to 10,000 files of metadata, the same cap as a Metadata API deploy.
questions.f: An inbound or outbound change set can hold up to 5,000 files of metadata, half the cap of a Metadata API deploy.
questions.x: Change sets share the Metadata API's per-operation limit of 10,000 files. The 5,000-file figure is wrong, and the two tools do not have different caps.

questions.t: Deploying a change set that contains Apex to production runs all local tests by default, but deploying it to a sandbox runs no tests automatically.
questions.f: Deploying a change set that contains Apex runs all local tests by default, whether the target is production or a sandbox.
questions.x: Local tests run by default only when the target is production; sandbox deployments skip automatic test runs. The false statement wrongly extends the production behaviour to sandboxes.

questions.t: DevOps Center's Analytics tab reports DORA metrics that can be viewed for up to 90 days.
questions.f: DevOps Center's Analytics tab reports DORA metrics that can be viewed for up to 30 days.
questions.x: DORA metrics in the Analytics tab cover a window of up to 90 days. The 30-day figure belongs to the separate Agentforce Vibes activity dashboard, not to DORA metrics.

questions.t: In a DevOps Center pipeline, each stage has its own source control branch, and promotion merges it into the next stage's branch before deploying.
questions.f: In a DevOps Center pipeline, all stages share one source control branch, and promotion deploys that branch straight to the next stage's org.
questions.x: Every pipeline stage maps to its own branch; promoting merges the current stage's branch into the next one and then deploys to that stage's org. Stages do not share a single branch.

questions.t: DevOps Center is unavailable in both Government Cloud Plus and the EU Operating Zone.
questions.f: DevOps Center is available in Government Cloud Plus but unavailable in the EU Operating Zone.
questions.x: Neither Government Cloud Plus nor the EU Operating Zone supports it, and Help warns that enabling the managed package in Government Cloud Plus can move data outside the authorization boundary.

questions.t: A Metadata API deploy or retrieve .zip can be at most 39 MB compressed and 600 MB uncompressed.
questions.f: A Metadata API deploy or retrieve .zip can be at most 50 MB compressed and 600 MB uncompressed.
questions.x: The compressed cap is 39 MB, set below the 50 MB SOAP message limit because base-64 encoding inflates the payload. 50 MB is the SOAP message limit, not the .zip cap.

questions.t: RunLocalTests is the default test level for Metadata API production deployments that contain Apex.
questions.f: RunAllTestsInOrg is the default test level for Metadata API production deployments that contain Apex.
questions.x: Production deployments with Apex default to RunLocalTests, which skips tests from installed managed and unlocked packages. RunAllTestsInOrg must be chosen explicitly.

questions.t: With the RunSpecifiedTests test level, each class and trigger in a deployment needs at least 75% code coverage on its own.
questions.f: With the RunSpecifiedTests test level, only the aggregate code coverage across the whole deployment needs to reach 75%.
questions.x: RunSpecifiedTests is stricter than an aggregate check: every class and trigger must individually reach 75% coverage from the named tests, so a high overall average is not enough.

questions.t: For CI, the recommended Salesforce CLI login is the JWT flow, which needs a certificate, its private key and an external client app.
questions.f: For CI, the recommended Salesforce CLI login is the web flow, which opens a browser and uses the default Salesforce CLI connected app.
questions.x: The JWT flow runs headless and is the recommended CI option. The web flow opens a browser, so it suits interactive work rather than unattended pipelines.

questions.t: Just-in-time Salesforce CLI plugins, such as code-analyzer, install automatically the first time one of their commands runs.
questions.f: Just-in-time Salesforce CLI plugins, such as code-analyzer, must be installed manually with sf plugins install before their first use.
questions.x: Just-in-time plugins are fetched automatically on first use and then kept current by sf update. Manual sf plugins install is how user-installed plugins are added.

questions.t: The Salesforce CLI stable channel is released weekly, with a release candidate shipped alongside each stable release.
questions.f: The Salesforce CLI stable channel is released monthly, with a release candidate shipped alongside each stable release.
questions.x: Stable releases come out every week, each paired with a release candidate, while nightly builds are daily. A monthly cadence understates how often the CLI changes.

questions.t: A connected app's Permitted Users policy defaults to All users may self-authorize, so each user approves the app on first use.
questions.f: A connected app's Permitted Users policy defaults to Admin approved users are pre-authorized, so access comes only from profiles or permission sets.
questions.x: Self-authorization is the default; admin-approved access must be chosen explicitly, and switching to it immediately cuts off users without a profile or permission set grant.

questions.t: The Use Any API Client permission lets a user reach any connected app, even one restricted to admin-approved users.
questions.f: The Use Any API Client permission lets a user reach any self-authorize connected app, but not one restricted to admin-approved users.
questions.x: This permission bypasses the admin-approved restriction entirely, which is why holders of it should be audited. It is not limited to self-authorize apps.

questions.t: Tightening a connected app's refresh token policy does not end active sessions, because the policy is checked only when a refresh token is used.
questions.f: Tightening a connected app's refresh token policy ends active sessions at once, because the policy is checked on every API request.
questions.x: The refresh token policy is evaluated only at the moment a refresh token is exchanged, so existing sessions keep running until then. It is not checked on each request.

questions.t: When a sandbox is created or refreshed, only packaged external client apps are copied into it, not local ones.
questions.f: When a sandbox is created or refreshed, both local and packaged external client apps are copied into it.
questions.x: Local external client apps stay in their home org and are skipped by sandbox copies; only packaged ones come across, so sandbox setup has to account for that.

questions.t: In an external client app, the subscriber admin's Policies stay local and are never packaged, while the developer's Settings travel in the package.
questions.f: In an external client app, the developer's Settings stay local and are never packaged, while the subscriber admin's Policies travel in the package.
questions.x: Developers own the Settings, which ship in the package; subscriber admins own the Policies, which they tune per org and which are never packaged. The false version reverses the roles.

questions.t: An external client app's global OAuth settings should be kept out of the package, in a long-lived org such as the Dev Hub.
questions.f: An external client app's global OAuth settings should be included in the package, so every subscriber org holds its own copy.
questions.x: Global OAuth settings, which hold the consumer details, belong in a non-ephemeral org that outlives the packages, such as the Dev Hub. Packaging them is explicitly discouraged.

questions.t: Without the Change Data Capture add-on, an org can select at most 5 entities for change events across all channels.
questions.f: Without the Change Data Capture add-on, an org can select at most 50 entities for change events across all channels.
questions.x: The base allocation caps selected entities at 5 across all channels; the add-on removes that cap. 50 is not the base limit.

questions.t: An Apex change event trigger receives batches of up to 2,000 change event messages by default.
questions.f: An Apex change event trigger receives batches of up to 200 change event messages by default.
questions.x: Change event triggers run asynchronously after commit and take up to 2,000 messages per batch by default, ten times the 200 stated in the false version.

questions.t: Change Data Capture applies field-level security to what a subscriber receives, but it does not apply sharing settings.
questions.f: Change Data Capture applies sharing settings to what a subscriber receives, but it does not apply field-level security.
questions.x: Field-level security restricts which fields a subscriber sees, while record sharing is not enforced on change events. The false version swaps the two.

questions.t: Creating a custom object in Salesforce stores its definition as metadata instead of creating a new physical database table.
questions.f: Creating a custom object in Salesforce runs DDL that creates a new physical database table for that object.
questions.x: The platform keeps object definitions as metadata and materializes them at runtime, so schema changes need no locks or downtime. No per-object table is created.

questions.t: In SalesforceDB the tenant ID is part of the primary key, which clusters each tenant's data together in a shared database.
questions.f: In SalesforceDB each tenant gets its own separate physical database, which keeps each tenant's data together.
questions.x: One instance runs a single shared database and schema; isolation comes from the tenant ID in the primary key, tenant predicates on queries and per-tenant encryption keys, not separate databases.

questions.t: Salesforce's query optimizer keeps tenant-, group- and user-level statistics and runs pre-queries to measure selectivity before choosing a plan.
questions.f: Salesforce's query optimizer keeps only table-level statistics shared by all tenants and picks a plan without measuring selectivity first.
questions.x: Conventional statistics ignore what each user can see, so the platform tracks statistics per tenant, group and user and checks selectivity with pre-queries before planning.

questions.t: During a record save, before-save record-triggered flows run before all before triggers.
questions.f: During a record save, before-save record-triggered flows run after all before triggers.
questions.x: The server runs before-save flows first and then the before triggers, all ahead of custom validation. The false version reverses that order.

questions.t: A workflow field update fires before-update and after-update triggers once more, but custom validation rules do not run again.
questions.f: A workflow field update runs custom validation rules once more, but before-update and after-update triggers do not fire again.
questions.x: The extra save caused by a workflow field update re-fires update triggers, even for an original insert, while custom validation, flows and duplicate rules are skipped on that pass.

questions.t: Record-triggered flows with no trigger order value run after flows numbered 1 to 1,000 and before flows numbered 1,001 to 2,000.
questions.f: Record-triggered flows with no trigger order value run after all flows numbered 1 to 2,000.
questions.x: Numbered flows 1 to 1,000 go first, then unnumbered flows by activation date, then 1,001 to 2,000. Unnumbered flows are not pushed to the very end.

questions.t: Buying a Full sandbox add-on also brings 15 extra Developer sandboxes.
questions.f: Buying a Full sandbox add-on also brings 5 extra Developer sandboxes.
questions.x: Each paid sandbox add-on comes with bonus Developer sandboxes: 5 with Developer Pro, 10 with Partial Copy and 15 with Full. Five is the Developer Pro bonus, not the Full one.

questions.t: A sandbox template is required when creating a Partial Copy sandbox and optional when creating a Full sandbox.
questions.f: A sandbox template is required when creating a Full sandbox and optional when creating a Partial Copy sandbox.
questions.x: Partial Copy sandboxes need a template to choose the sample data, while a Full sandbox copies all data and can take a template only optionally. The false version reverses them.

questions.t: A sandbox that nobody logs into for 180 days becomes eligible for deletion, and a deleted sandbox cannot be recovered.
questions.f: A sandbox that nobody logs into for 365 days becomes eligible for deletion, and a deleted sandbox cannot be recovered.
questions.x: Salesforce flags sandboxes with no logins for 180 days as eligible for deletion, and deletion is permanent. A full year of inactivity is longer than the actual threshold.

questions.t: Salesforce Government Cloud Plus holds a FedRAMP authorization at the High security impact level, granted through the Joint Authorization Board.
questions.f: Salesforce Government Cloud Plus holds a FedRAMP authorization at the Moderate security impact level, granted through the Joint Authorization Board.
questions.x: Government Cloud Plus launched with a FedRAMP High provisional ATO from the JAB and is listed at the High impact level on the FedRAMP Marketplace. Moderate is the wrong impact level.

questions.t: MuleSoft Government Cloud Plus permits only connectors that are tagged as FIPS 140-3 verified.
questions.f: MuleSoft Government Cloud Plus permits any Anypoint connector, as long as the Private Space has outbound internet access turned on.
questions.x: MuleSoft's government control plane restricts connectors to those tagged FIPS 140-3 verified. Enabling outbound access does not lift that restriction, so arbitrary connectors are not allowed.

questions.t: Government Cloud Plus's FedRAMP High authorization covers the service boundary, so each agency still issues its own ATO against the package.
questions.f: Government Cloud Plus's FedRAMP High authorization acts as a blanket ATO, so agencies no longer issue their own ATO against the package.
questions.x: The FedRAMP authorization applies to Salesforce's boundary, not to an agency's org; the dozens of ATO letters on the Marketplace are separate agency decisions. It is not a blanket ATO for every customer.

questions.t: When preparing a Public Sector Solutions org, person accounts should be enabled before OmniStudio is installed.
questions.f: When preparing a Public Sector Solutions org, person accounts should be enabled only after OmniStudio is installed.
questions.x: Trailhead's org-prep guidance says to turn on person accounts first and install OmniStudio afterwards. Reversing that order goes against the recommended setup sequence.

questions.t: In Public Sector Solutions, the Business Rules Engine automates eligibility and fee decisions using expression sets and decision matrices.
questions.f: In Public Sector Solutions, Action Plans automate eligibility and fee decisions using expression sets and decision matrices.
questions.x: Eligibility and fee logic is handled by the Business Rules Engine, with Decision Explainer showing why a rule fired. Action Plans supply task checklists for inspections or reviews, not rules evaluation.

questions.t: Under Public Sector Solutions usage-based pricing, application record types left unmapped default to License and Permit Management, which can inflate usage counts.
questions.f: Under Public Sector Solutions usage-based pricing, application record types left unmapped default to Grants Management, which can inflate usage counts.
questions.x: The admin guide warns that unmapped application record types fall back to License and Permit Management. Grants Management is not the default bucket.

questions.t: Salesforce orgs created in Spring '21 or later can have up to 5,000 roles, while older orgs start at 500.
questions.f: Salesforce orgs created in Spring '21 or later can have up to 10,000 roles, while older orgs start at 1,000.
questions.x: The sharing architecture guide gives 5,000 roles for newer orgs and 500 for older ones, which can request more from Support. The 10,000 and 1,000 figures are inflated.

questions.t: The Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting can be cleared only for custom objects; for standard objects, hierarchy access is always on.
questions.f: The Grant Access Using Hierarchies setting can be cleared only for standard objects; for custom objects, hierarchy access is always on.
questions.x: Standard objects always grant access up the role hierarchy, while custom objects expose a checkbox (checked by default) that can switch it off. The false statement reverses the two.

questions.t: Salesforce recommends keeping the role hierarchy to no more than 10 levels of branches.
questions.f: Salesforce recommends keeping the role hierarchy to no more than 25 levels of branches.
questions.x: Salesforce's sharing architecture guidance suggests a maximum depth of about 10 branch levels. Twenty-five levels is well beyond that recommendation.

questions.t: Manual sharing is offered only when an object's organization-wide default is Private or Public Read Only.
questions.f: Manual sharing is offered only when an object's organization-wide default is Public Read/Write or Controlled by Parent.
questions.x: Manual sharing opens a record beyond the baseline, so it is only available when the default is restrictive: Private or Public Read Only. With Public Read/Write there is nothing more to open.

questions.t: When a record's owner changes, its manual shares are deleted, but its Apex managed shares are kept.
questions.f: When a record's owner changes, its Apex managed shares are deleted, but its manual shares are kept.
questions.x: Apex managed shares survive an ownership change or owner deactivation, while user-managed manual shares are removed when the owner changes. The false statement swaps which kind persists.

questions.t: Full Access to a record can come only from managed sharing such as ownership; a manual share is limited to lower access levels.
questions.f: Full Access to a record can be granted through a manual share, in addition to managed sharing such as ownership.
questions.x: Full Access (the All level) is reserved for platform-managed grants like ownership. Manual shares cannot hand it out, so the false statement overstates what manual sharing can do.

questions.t: Salesforce's large-data-volume guidance recommends archiving or discarding data at the rate it arrives, so the active record set stays roughly constant.
questions.f: Salesforce's large-data-volume guidance recommends archiving data in one annual clean-up once storage limits are reached, letting the active set grow in between.
questions.x: The LDV best practices say to remove data at the rate it comes in so performance does not degrade as volume grows. Infrequent, limit-driven clean-ups are what a deliberate archiving strategy is meant to replace.

questions.t: Custom big objects used as an archive enforce object and field permissions, but they do not support sharing rules, triggers or flows.
questions.f: Custom big objects used as an archive enforce object and field permissions and support sharing rules and flows, but not triggers.
questions.x: Big objects scale to billions of records but only honour object and field permissions; sharing rules, triggers and flows are all unsupported. Claiming sharing rules and flows work is wrong.

questions.t: In Salesforce Archive, master-detail children are archived with their parent automatically, while lookup children are included only through configuration.
questions.f: In Salesforce Archive, lookup children are archived with their parent automatically, while master-detail children are included only through configuration.
questions.x: Salesforce Archive keeps relationships intact by moving master-detail children along with the parent by default; lookup children must be added in the policy. The false statement swaps the two relationship types.

questions.t: Salesforce's loading guidance recommends Bulk API 2.0 for operations above 2,000 records and bulkified synchronous calls below that.
questions.f: Salesforce's loading guidance recommends Bulk API 2.0 for operations above 50,000 records and bulkified synchronous calls below that.
questions.x: The large-data-volume loading guide sets the Bulk API 2.0 threshold at 2,000 records, using REST Composite or SOAP below it. 50,000 is not the stated cutoff.

questions.t: For migration loads, insert is the fastest operation, followed by update, with upsert the slowest.
questions.f: For migration loads, upsert is the fastest operation, followed by update, with insert the slowest.
questions.x: Insert is quickest and upsert slowest, so the guidance suggests splitting upserts into separate create and update passes where possible. The false ordering is reversed.

questions.t: During a large initial load, set target objects' org-wide defaults to Public Read/Write so no sharing rows are computed, then tighten them afterward.
questions.f: During a large initial load, set target objects' org-wide defaults to Private so no sharing rows are computed, then open them up afterward.
questions.x: Public Read/Write avoids sharing calculations while data streams in; defaults are tightened to Private or Public Read Only once the load is done. Private during the load is what generates the sharing work.

questions.t: To start an autolaunched flow from a record page layout, use a custom button, because actions can call only screen flows.
questions.f: To start an autolaunched flow from a record page layout, use an action, because custom buttons can call only screen flows.
questions.x: Actions look like buttons but can launch only screen flows, so a screenless autolaunched flow needs a custom button. The false statement reverses which one is restricted.

questions.t: Autolaunched and screen flows can be called as subflows, but record-triggered flows cannot be referenced from another flow.
questions.f: Autolaunched and record-triggered flows can be called as subflows, but screen flows cannot be referenced from another flow.
questions.x: Both autolaunched and screen flows work as subflows; record-triggered flows cannot be called from a parent flow. That is why shared logic usually lives in an autolaunched flow.

questions.t: If an autolaunched flow element exceeds a governor limit, the whole transaction rolls back even when that element has a fault connector.
questions.f: If an autolaunched flow element exceeds a governor limit and has a fault connector, only that element's work rolls back and the flow follows the fault path.
questions.x: Limit breaches cannot be caught by a fault connector; the entire transaction is rolled back. The false statement treats a limit breach like an ordinary handled fault.

questions.t: An approval process's default submission action locks the record so that only approvers and admins can edit it while the request is pending.
questions.f: An approval process's default submission action locks the record so that only the submitter and admins can edit it while the request is pending.
questions.x: By default, submitting for approval locks the record, leaving edit rights with approvers and administrators. The submitter is not the one who keeps edit access.

questions.t: Salesforce Help calls before-save flows the best-performing record-triggered option, because they are limited to updating the triggering record.
questions.f: Salesforce Help calls after-save flows the best-performing record-triggered option, because they are limited to updating the triggering record.
questions.x: Before-save (fast field update) flows change the triggering record inside the original save without an extra DML, which is why Salesforce rates them fastest. After-save flows can touch other records and need additional DML, so they are not the fastest option.

questions.t: Automation on the after-undelete event must be built with an Apex trigger, because record-triggered flows do not support that event.
questions.f: Automation on the after-undelete event must be built with a record-triggered flow, because Apex triggers do not support that event.
questions.x: Flow has no after-undelete support, which leaves Apex triggers as the only option for that event. The false statement swaps which tool handles it.

questions.t: A top-level screen flow runs in user context by default, so the running user's object and field permissions apply.
questions.f: A top-level screen flow runs in system context without sharing by default, so the running user's object and field permissions are ignored.
questions.x: Screen flows default to user context, applying the launching user's profile and permission sets; system context is an opt-in choice, and system without sharing is meant to be used sparingly.

questions.t: Reactive screen components in a screen flow require the flow to use API version 59.0 or later.
questions.f: Reactive screen components in a screen flow require the flow to use API version 52.0 or later.
questions.x: Salesforce ties screen-flow reactivity to API version 59.0 or later; 52.0 is too early a version for the feature.

questions.t: In a reactive screen flow, the $Flow global variable is reactive, while $Organization, $Profile and custom labels are not.
questions.f: In a reactive screen flow, the $Profile global variable is reactive, while $Flow, $Organization and custom labels are not.
questions.x: Only $Flow reacts to changes on the screen; $Organization, $Profile, custom labels and custom settings do not, so the false statement swaps the one reactive global variable.

questions.t: Changes to an LWR Experience Cloud site appear to visitors only after the site is republished, because its components are fixed at publish time.
questions.f: Changes to an Aura Experience Cloud site appear to visitors only after the site is republished, because its components are fixed at publish time.
questions.x: LWR sites freeze their components when published and serve them as static content, so edits need a republish; that publish-time behaviour is the LWR difference, not an Aura one.

questions.t: The Customer Community license has no roles or sharing rules, so sites built on it rely on sharing sets to give users record access.
questions.f: The Partner Community license has no roles or sharing rules, so sites built on it rely on sharing sets to give users record access.
questions.x: Customer Community is the high-volume tier without roles or sharing rules, which is why it depends on sharing sets; Partner Community includes roles, sharing rules and reports.

questions.t: With secure guest user record access enabled, guest users' org-wide defaults are fixed at Private and only sharing rules can grant them record access.
questions.f: With secure guest user record access enabled, guest users' org-wide defaults are fixed at Public Read Only and sharing sets can grant them record access.
questions.x: Secure guest access locks guest defaults to Private and allows only sharing rules to open records to them; neither Public Read Only defaults nor sharing sets apply.

questions.t: Collaborative Forecasts allows only four forecast types to be active at a time; more require a request to Salesforce Customer Support.
questions.f: Collaborative Forecasts allows only ten forecast types to be active at a time; more require a request to Salesforce Customer Support.
questions.x: The active forecast type limit is four, and going beyond it means contacting Customer Support; ten is not the stated limit.

questions.t: Changing the rollup setting in Collaborative Forecasts deletes existing forecast adjustments for all active forecast types.
questions.f: Changing the rollup setting in Collaborative Forecasts deletes existing forecast adjustments only for the forecast type being edited.
questions.x: The rollup setting applies across forecasting, so changing it wipes adjustments for every active forecast type, not just one.

questions.t: When person accounts are enabled, converting a lead that has no company name creates a person account.
questions.f: When person accounts are enabled, converting a lead that has no company name creates a business account named after the lead.
questions.x: With person accounts on, a lead without a company name converts into a person account; a business account is created from the company name, which this lead lacks.

questions.t: In Data 360, ingested or federated data first lands in data lake objects in its source shape, before mapping to data model objects.
questions.f: In Data 360, ingested or federated data first lands in data model objects in its source shape, before mapping to data lake objects.
questions.x: Data lake objects are the raw landing containers; their fields are then mapped onto the Customer 360 Data Model to form data model objects, so the false statement reverses the order.

questions.t: Accelerated Query caching in Data 360 keeps a local copy of federated data refreshed between every 15 minutes and every 7 days.
questions.f: Accelerated Query caching in Data 360 keeps a local copy of federated data refreshed between every 1 minute and every 24 hours.
questions.x: The cache refresh interval ranges from 15 minutes to 7 days; the 1-minute to 24-hour range is not what Salesforce states.

questions.t: An incremental cache refresh in Data 360 only upserts, so deleted source records stay in the cache until a full refresh runs.
questions.f: An incremental cache refresh in Data 360 upserts and deletes, so deleted source records are removed from the cache on the next refresh.
questions.x: Incremental refresh only inserts and updates; deletions are picked up only by a full refresh, so stale deleted rows can linger in the cache.

questions.t: Einstein Trust Layer data masking can be enabled for embedded features such as Work Summaries, but it is disabled for agents.
questions.f: Einstein Trust Layer data masking can be enabled for agents, but it is disabled for embedded features such as Work Summaries.
questions.x: Admins can turn masking on for embedded features like Service Replies and Work Summaries, while agents run with masking disabled, so agent designs must lean on permissions and grounding scope.

questions.t: Einstein Trust Layer audit and feedback data is stored in Data Cloud data model objects such as GenAIGatewayRequest.
questions.f: Einstein Trust Layer audit and feedback data is stored in Event Monitoring log files such as GenAIGatewayRequest.
questions.x: The audit trail and feedback land in Data Cloud data model objects and are analysed with Data Cloud tools like the Query Editor, not in Event Monitoring logs.

questions.t: The Trust Layer's toxicity check rolls category scores into one score between 0 and 1, where a higher score means more toxic.
questions.f: The Trust Layer's toxicity check rolls category scores into one score between 0 and 100, where a lower score means more toxic.
questions.x: Toxicity results are combined into a single 0-to-1 score where higher values indicate more toxic content; the scale is not 0 to 100 and the direction is not inverted.

questions.t: On a junction object, the first master-detail field created becomes the primary relationship and supplies the junction's owner, page colour and icon.
questions.f: On a junction object, the second master-detail field created becomes the primary relationship and supplies the junction's owner, page colour and icon.
questions.x: Creation order decides primacy: the first master-detail field is primary, and junction records take their owner and look from that primary master; the second field is secondary.

questions.t: When both master records of a junction record are deleted, the junction record is removed permanently rather than sent to the Recycle Bin.
questions.f: When both master records of a junction record are deleted, the junction record is sent to the Recycle Bin rather than removed permanently.
questions.x: Deleting one master sends its junction records to the Recycle Bin, but deleting both masters removes the junction record permanently.

questions.t: A parent with more than 200 junction records can't be deleted while the junction has a roll-up summary field rolling up to the other parent.
questions.f: A parent with more than 2,000 junction records can't be deleted while the junction has a roll-up summary field rolling up to the other parent.
questions.x: The deletion block applies above 200 junction records when a roll-up to the other parent exists; the junction records must be deleted first. The threshold is 200, not 2,000.

questions.t: A single Apex request can carry anywhere from 1 to 50,000 records, so code must be bulkified rather than written one record at a time.
questions.f: A single Apex request can carry anywhere from 1 to 200 records, so code must be bulkified rather than written one record at a time.
questions.x: Salesforce says a request may contain 1 to 50,000 records, which is why record-by-record code hits governor limits; 200 understates the range.

questions.t: Unlike Java, Apex is case-insensitive and adds a global access modifier that exposes code across namespaces.
questions.f: Like Java, Apex is case-sensitive and adds a global access modifier that exposes code across namespaces.
questions.x: Apex differs from Java by ignoring case in identifiers and keywords; the global modifier for cross-namespace exposure is an Apex addition, but case sensitivity is not shared with Java.

questions.t: When Apex is saved, the server compiles it into an abstract instruction set stored as metadata and run by the Apex runtime interpreter.
questions.f: When Apex is saved, the server compiles it into JavaScript stored as metadata and run in the user's browser when the code is invoked.
questions.x: Apex never runs on the client: saving compiles it into instructions kept as metadata, which the server's interpreter executes when an action invokes the code.

questions.t: Dev Hub can't be enabled in a sandbox, and once enabled in an org it can't be turned off.
questions.f: Dev Hub can be enabled in a full sandbox, and once enabled in an org it can be turned off again.
questions.x: Dev Hub is enabled in a production, Developer Edition or trial org, never a sandbox, and the switch is one-way; the false twin allows a sandbox and claims it is reversible.

questions.t: Dev Hub can be enabled in Developer, Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited editions, but it can't be enabled in a sandbox.
questions.f: Dev Hub can be enabled in a full sandbox as well as in Developer, Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited editions.
questions.x: Dev Hub must live in a production or Developer Edition org of a supported edition; sandboxes are excluded. It also can't be turned off once enabled.

questions.t: In a Salesforce DX project, custom objects are decomposed into subdirectories by default to ease navigation and reduce merge conflicts.
questions.f: In a Salesforce DX project, custom objects stay as one large file by default and are decomposed only after opting in with sourceBehaviorOptions.
questions.x: Source format splits custom objects and their translations into subfolders out of the box. The opt-in sourceBehaviorOptions setting is for other types, such as permission sets and custom labels.

questions.t: In sfdx-project.json, only one packageDirectories entry can be the default, and that directory receives retrieved changes.
questions.f: In sfdx-project.json, several packageDirectories entries can be marked default, and retrieved changes are split across them.
questions.x: The packageDirectories list is required and allows exactly one default directory. That default gets retrieved source and is used for second-generation packages.

questions.t: A scratch org's lifespan can be set from 1 to 30 days with --duration-days, and it defaults to 7 days.
questions.f: A scratch org's lifespan can be set from 1 to 90 days with --duration-days, and it defaults to 30 days.
questions.x: The CLI accepts a duration between 1 and 30 days and uses 7 when none is given. After expiry the org is gone for good.

questions.t: An Enterprise Edition Dev Hub allows 40 active scratch orgs and 80 scratch org creations per day.
questions.f: An Enterprise Edition Dev Hub allows 100 active scratch orgs and 200 scratch org creations per day.
questions.x: Enterprise Dev Hubs get 40 active and 80 daily. The 100 active and 200 daily allocation belongs to Unlimited and Performance editions.

questions.t: Deleting a scratch org frees an active slot, but its creation still counts against the Dev Hub's daily allocation.
questions.f: Deleting a scratch org frees an active slot and also refunds its creation from the Dev Hub's daily allocation.
questions.x: Active and daily limits are tracked separately. The daily count is a rolling 24-hour tally of successful creations, so deletion doesn't give it back.

questions.t: A managed 2GP package version can be promoted to released only if code coverage was computed and is at least 75%.
questions.f: A managed 2GP package version can be promoted to released only if code coverage was computed and is at least 50%.
questions.x: Promotion requires a version created with code coverage calculated and at least 75% Apex coverage, with every trigger covered. Versions built with --skip-validation can't be promoted.

questions.t: Several managed 2GP packages can share one namespace, and Salesforce advises using a single namespace across a partner's packages.
questions.f: Each managed 2GP package needs its own namespace, so a partner's packages can't share one namespace.
questions.x: Sharing a namespace across packages is a key change from 1GP. Salesforce recommends one namespace for all of a partner's packages because it simplifies sharing code between them.

questions.t: A beta version of a managed 2GP package can't be upgraded, so betas should be kept out of sandboxes in the release pipeline.
questions.f: A beta version of a managed 2GP package can be upgraded in place to a released version, so betas are safe in pipeline sandboxes.
questions.x: Package versions start as beta and must be promoted to become managed-released. An installed beta has no upgrade path, which makes it a dead end in any org you plan to keep.

questions.t: Among sandboxes, source tracking is supported only in Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes, not in Partial Copy or Full sandboxes.
questions.f: Among sandboxes, source tracking is supported in every sandbox type, including Partial Copy and Full sandboxes.
questions.x: Tracking can be enabled only in the two developer sandbox types. For Partial Copy, Full or other untracked orgs, metadata has to be moved explicitly with manifests or packages.

questions.t: The Dev Hub setting that enables source tracking in sandboxes applies only to sandboxes created or refreshed after it is turned on.
questions.f: The Dev Hub setting that enables source tracking in sandboxes applies at once to all existing sandboxes, with no refresh needed.
questions.x: The org-wide switch in production affects sandboxes created or refreshed afterward, so existing ones need a refresh. The per-sandbox setting is the alternative and tracks only later changes.

questions.t: Salesforce CLI learns what changed in an org for source tracking by reading the SourceMember object through the Tooling API.
questions.f: Salesforce CLI learns what changed in an org for source tracking by reading the Setup Audit Trail through the Metadata API.
questions.x: After a deployment the CLI waits for SourceMember, a Tooling API object, to update and reads it to detect server-side changes. Deployments themselves still go through the Metadata API.

questions.t: On an external credential, a named principal uses one identity for the whole org, while a per-user principal authenticates each user individually.
questions.f: On an external credential, a per-user principal uses one identity for the whole org, while a named principal authenticates each user individually.
questions.x: Named principals share a single org-wide identity; per-user principals hold each user's own authentication. Either way, the running user needs a mapped permission set or profile to call out.

questions.t: Access tokens and other named credential secrets can't be packaged, so they must be populated after install through Setup or the Connect API.
questions.f: Access tokens and other named credential secrets are packaged with the credential, so they arrive populated after install.
questions.x: Packages carry the credential definitions but not the secrets. Release plans need a step to fill in tokens in each target org.

questions.t: Creating, editing or deleting named credentials requires the Manage Named Credentials or Customize Applications permission.
questions.f: Creating, editing or deleting named credentials requires the Modify All Data or Author Apex permission.
questions.x: Credential administration is gated by Manage Named Credentials or Customize Applications, while just viewing them needs View Setup and Configuration.

questions.t: During a scheduled Hyperforce migration, a production org is read-only for about three hours.
questions.f: During a scheduled Hyperforce migration, a production org is read-only for about 24 hours.
questions.x: The cutover makes production read-only for roughly three hours inside the Preferred Maintenance Window. Sandboxes are fully inaccessible during their window.

questions.t: On Hyperforce, mission-critical services and data are replicated across at least three availability zones.
questions.f: On Hyperforce, mission-critical services and data are replicated across at least two availability zones.
questions.x: Hyperforce's resilience design keeps critical services and data in a minimum of three availability zones, and backups go to other Hyperforce instances.

questions.t: In Hyperforce, a cell is the unit formerly called an instance or pod, acting as both a scale unit and a blast-radius boundary.
questions.f: In Hyperforce, a grid is the unit formerly called an instance or pod, acting as both a scale unit and a blast-radius boundary.
questions.x: A cell holds one or more orgs and limits the impact of failures. A grid is a larger grouping of Hyperforce instances that share a control plane.

questions.t: An Apex transaction trying to lock a record already locked by another transaction waits up to 10 seconds before an exception is thrown.
questions.f: An Apex transaction trying to lock a record already locked by another transaction waits up to 60 seconds before an exception is thrown.
questions.x: The lock wait is capped at 10 seconds, after which a QueryException or DmlException is raised; API clients see this as UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW.

questions.t: Making a callout automatically releases any record locks taken with SOQL FOR UPDATE in that transaction.
questions.f: Making a callout keeps record locks taken with SOQL FOR UPDATE in place until the transaction commits.
questions.x: A callout drops FOR UPDATE locks and logs a FOR_UPDATE_LOCKS_RELEASE event, so a lock, callout, update sequence loses its protection. Keep callouts out of the locked window.

questions.t: If more than 100 records in a Bulk API batch can't get locks, the rest of the batch is requeued, up to 10 times before it fails.
questions.f: If more than 100 records in a Bulk API batch can't get locks, the rest of the batch is requeued, up to 3 times before it fails.
questions.x: Bulk API retries the remainder of a lock-starved batch as many as 10 times before marking it permanently failed. Individual failed records are not retried and must be resubmitted.

questions.t: In each seasonal release, Salesforce upgrades sandboxes 4 to 6 weeks before it upgrades production orgs.
questions.f: In each seasonal release, Salesforce upgrades sandboxes 1 to 2 weeks after it upgrades production orgs.
questions.x: Sandboxes get the new release first, several weeks ahead of production, giving teams time to test. Customers can't choose their own upgrade date.

questions.t: Metadata is copied into every sandbox, but data is copied only into Full and Partial Copy sandboxes.
questions.f: Both metadata and data are copied into every sandbox, including Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes.
questions.x: Metadata and data follow different lifecycles. Every sandbox gets the org's metadata, while only Full and Partial Copy sandboxes receive data.

questions.t: Custom metadata types are metadata that can be packaged and deployed, whereas custom settings are data.
questions.f: Custom settings are metadata that can be packaged and deployed, whereas custom metadata types are data.
questions.x: Custom metadata records travel with deployments and packages. Custom settings values are data, so they have to be loaded separately in each org.

questions.t: DoD Impact Level 5 is built on the FedRAMP High baseline, while Impact Level 4 starts from FedRAMP Moderate.
questions.f: DoD Impact Level 5 is built on the FedRAMP Moderate baseline, while Impact Level 4 starts from FedRAMP Low.
questions.x: IL4 adds DoD controls on top of FedRAMP Moderate. IL5, which covers higher-sensitivity CUI and unclassified NSS data, uses FedRAMP High as its base.

questions.t: At IL5, cloud providers must physically separate federal tenants from non-federal tenants such as state and local governments.
questions.f: At IL5, cloud providers may host federal tenants alongside state and local governments using only logical separation.
questions.x: IL5 accepts logical separation between DoD and other federal tenants, but non-federal tenants must be physically separated. Shared hardware with virtual separation is allowed only at IL4.

questions.t: A DISA provisional authorization is a pre-approval; each mission owner's authorizing official still issues its own Authority to Operate.
questions.f: A DISA provisional authorization serves as the Authority to Operate for every DoD mission owner using that cloud offering.
questions.x: DISA grants a provisional authorization to a specific cloud offering. Each mission owner still assesses its own risk and grants an ATO, so an org inherits controls but isn't authorized on its own.

questions.t: Salesforce's large-data-volume guidance advises keeping any one user from owning more than 10,000 records.
questions.f: Salesforce's large-data-volume guidance advises keeping any one user from owning more than 100,000 records.
questions.x: Ownership concentration drives sharing computation and locking cost, so the guidance sets 10,000 records per owner, the same figure it uses for children under one parent.

questions.t: Salesforce's data-integration guidance defaults to minimising replication, accessing data in place through virtualization such as Salesforce Connect.
questions.f: Salesforce's data-integration guidance defaults to replicating external data into the org, using virtualization such as Salesforce Connect only as a last resort.
questions.x: The guide asks each project to name a source of truth and avoid copying records that don't need to live in the org; virtualization is the preferred way to reach them.

questions.t: Salesforce's data-integration guidance warns against building an integration strategy on stewardship tools like Data Loader or the Data Import Wizard.
questions.f: Salesforce's data-integration guidance recommends building an integration strategy on stewardship tools like Data Loader or the Data Import Wizard.
questions.x: Data Loader and the Import Wizard are for data stewardship tasks. Integration tooling should be chosen by weighing the ESB or ETL estate, timing, skills, volume and platform limits.

questions.t: Passing Platform App Builder, Platform Data Architect, Platform Developer and Sharing and Visibility Architect grants the Application Architect credential.
questions.f: Passing Platform App Builder, Platform Data Architect, Platform Developer and Sharing and Visibility Architect grants the System Architect credential.
questions.x: Those four exams make up the Application Architect stack, focused on native features, data modelling and sharing. System Architect comes from a different set centred on integration, identity and deployment.

questions.t: System Architect is granted after passing Platform Developer, Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, Identity and Access Management Architect and Integration Architect.
questions.f: System Architect is granted after passing Platform Developer, Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, Identity and Access Management Architect and Platform Data Architect.
questions.x: The System Architect stack ends with Integration Architect, matching its focus on off-platform systems. Platform Data Architect belongs to the Application Architect stack instead.

questions.t: In the CTA review board exam, candidates have 180 minutes to design a solution and 45 minutes to present it.
questions.f: In the CTA review board exam, candidates have 60 minutes to design a solution and 30 minutes to present it.
questions.x: The full review board exam allows 180 minutes of design and 45 of presentation. The 60 and 30 minute timings belong to the shorter online review board evaluation that comes first.

questions.t: Salesforce Optimizer flags objects with more than 350 fields, although the per-object maximum can reach 800 depending on edition.
questions.f: Salesforce Optimizer flags objects with more than 100 fields, although the per-object maximum can reach 800 depending on edition.
questions.x: Optimizer treats 350 fields on one object as a warning sign well below the hard ceiling of up to 800. It also flags piles of sharing rules, flows and multiple triggers on one object.

questions.t: Well-Architected guidance warns that teams who never budget for debt repayment face a large refactoring project every 18 to 24 months.
questions.f: Well-Architected guidance warns that teams who never budget for debt repayment face a large refactoring project every 5 to 7 years.
questions.x: When debt goes unrecorded and sprints leave no room to fix it, the backlog resurfaces as a big refactor roughly every 18 to 24 months. Tracking debt and paying it down continuously avoids that.

questions.t: Well-Architected code guidance recommends thin triggers that delegate to handler classes, with SOQL centralised in selector classes.
questions.f: Well-Architected code guidance recommends keeping business logic in trigger bodies, with SOQL centralised in selector classes.
questions.x: Logic written directly in trigger files grows hard to test and is listed as an anti-pattern. Triggers should hand off to handlers, with logic in service classes and queries in selectors.

questions.t: Once Lightning Knowledge is enabled in an org, it can't be turned off, so it's wise to try it in a sandbox first.
questions.f: Once Lightning Knowledge is enabled in an org, it can be switched back to Classic Knowledge from Knowledge Settings at any time.
questions.x: Enabling Lightning Knowledge is a one-way switch. Because it can't be undone, Salesforce suggests testing it in a sandbox before production.

questions.t: In Lightning Knowledge, kinds of articles are modeled as record types on Knowledge__kav instead of separate article type objects.
questions.f: In Lightning Knowledge, each kind of article gets its own object pair, such as FAQ__kav, instead of a record type.
questions.x: Lightning Knowledge keeps all articles in Knowledge__ka and Knowledge__kav and uses record types to vary layouts. Separate per-type object pairs were the Classic article-type model.

questions.t: All internal users can read Knowledge articles by default, but creating and editing them requires the Knowledge User license.
questions.f: All internal users can create and edit Knowledge articles by default, but reading them requires the Knowledge User license.
questions.x: Reading is open to internal users; authoring needs the Knowledge User license, enabled with a checkbox on the user record.

questions.t: A Field Generation prompt template reaches users only after Dynamic Forms is enabled, the template is selected on the field and the page assigned.
questions.f: A Field Generation prompt template reaches users as soon as it is activated, with no change to the record page needed.
questions.x: Field Generation templates surface through the record page, so the page must use Dynamic Forms with the template set on the field. Users then click the Einstein icon to get a suggestion.

questions.t: Apex grounding for a prompt template is an @InvocableMethod whose capabilityType matches the template type.
questions.f: Apex grounding for a prompt template is an @AuraEnabled method whose capabilityType matches the template type.
questions.x: Grounding Apex uses an invocable method that takes a list of requests and returns a list of responses, with capabilityType tying it to the template type. It must be deployed before it shows up as a resource.

questions.t: Prompt templates run in Lightning Experience on Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited editions with an Einstein or Agentforce add-on.
